message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt n\rfloor .
\]

We analyze the prime divisors of \(n\).

Suppose \(p^a\mid n\) is a prime power.

### 1. If \(p\le m\)

Then \(p\mid m!\), so \(p\mid (m!)^{n!}\). In fact,

\[
v_p\bigl((m!)^{n!}\bigr)=n!\,v_p(m!)\ge n!\ge a,
\]

so \((m!)^{n!}\equiv 0\pmod{p^a}\). Since \(p^a\mid n\) and

\[
n\mid (m!)^{n!}+450,
\]

we must have

\[
450\equiv 0\pmod{p^a}.
\]

Thus every prime power of \(n\) coming from primes \(\le m\) divides

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

So such primes can only be \(2,3,5\), with exponents bounded as in \(450\).

### 2. If \(p>m\)

Then \(p\nmid m!\), so \(m!\) is invertible modulo \(p\). Since \(p\mid n\), we have \(p-1\le n\), hence \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod p.
\]

Therefore

\[
0\equiv (m!)^{n!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\pmod p.
\]

So

\[
p\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Thus any prime divisor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) must be \(11\) or \(41\).

Also, if \(p>m\), then \(n<(m+1)^2\le p^2\), so \(p^2\nmid n\). Hence \(11\) and \(41\) can appear only to the first power. They cannot both appear, because if \(11\mid n\), then \(11>m\), so \(m\le 10\), forcing \(n<121\), impossible if \(41\mid n\).

Therefore every possible \(n\) has one of the forms

\[
n=s,\qquad n=11s,\qquad n=41s,
\]

where \(s\mid 450\) is the part made from primes \(2,3,5\).

Now bound these cases:

- If \(n=s\), then \(n\mid 450\), so \(n\le 450\).
- If \(n=11s\), then \(11>m\), so \(m\le 10\) and \(n<121\). Thus \(s<11\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(11\) is \(10\), so \(n\le 110\).
- If \(n=41s\), then \(41>m\), so \(n<41^2\). Thus \(s<41\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\), so

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

Hence every valid \(n\) satisfies \(n\le 1230\).

Now check \(n=1230\). We have

\[
\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]

and

\[
1230=30\cdot 41.
\]

Since \(30\mid 35!\), we have

\[
30\mid (35!)^{1230!}.
\]

Also \(30\mid 450\), so

\[
30\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

For the factor \(41\), note that \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\). Thus by Fermat,

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Therefore

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), we get

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Thus the largest such positive integer is

\[
\boxed{1230}.
\]
